Breaking: 4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.
  • Industry observers note that have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year?
  • If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.

Industry observers note that have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year? Maybe.

But what about your money? If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?

According to recent reports, dan Stanush, senior financial planner at Charles Schwab in Asheville, North Carolina, recalls how fast financial conveniences disappeared after Hurricane Helene hit in 2024. “We lost power for three weeks and water for six weeks,” he remarked in an email. “And some local businesses could only accept cash or checks because card systems and ATMs were down.”.

Don’t get caught unprepared. Here are the moves experts suggest to help you weather various types of emergencies:.

Industry observers note that last week’s Chase outage was a good reminder that access to your bank balance can be disrupted. Stash at least enough cash at home — in small bills — to cover one week of expenses, notes Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner (CFP) with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland.

If systems go down, ATMs can go down with them, mentioned Eileen Olson, a CFP with Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, in an email. Keeping cash in a safe at home is a good initiative, but it’s also smart to carry cash when you travel. (Remember when planes were grounded nationwide a week and a half ago?).

“My parents and sister were traveling overseas on 9/11 and got stuck much longer than they expected,” Olson said. “After that, they always traveled with more cash.”.

If your primary bank and its app were down, would you be able to pay bills? Having an account at more than one bank gives you an alternate funding source. Consider opening a high-yield savings account at a second bank or credit union for your emergency fund.

“This is the step I push hardest,” Judge claims. “I had a client whose debit card, credit card and savings all ran through one bank, so when that bank’s system went down, she couldn’t even buy gas.”.

If you don’t want to open a second bank account, a second credit card from a different bank and preferably on a different network (i.e. Visa vs. Mastercard) can provide another way to pay for things. “If there’s a problem with one credit card network, I have a backup with two other credit cards,” says Tony Steuer, author of “Get Ready! A Step-by-Step Planner for Maintaining Your Financial First Aid Kit.”.

According to recent reports, make a printed list of your accounts, along with account numbers and key contact numbers. Include your bank, insurers, credit card companies and any financial professionals. Store the list with copies of essential paperwork, including insurance policies and their declarations pages, estate planning documents, legal certificates and identification — potentially in a fire-resistant file box.

In a recent development, keep a digital copy of your documents in a password-protected, encrypted spot as well. A password manager can store all of your login info.

Joon Um, a CFP with Secure Tax & Accounting in Beverly Hills, California, suggests digital storage site Everplans to his clients, but there are a variety of sites that offer encrypted document storage.

Take some time to write down how you’d pay for groceries, gas and medication if your usual payment methods weren’t available. What expenses would you need to cover first? What recurring bills are on autopay? Where would you keep the cash and any key documents you’d want to take with you if you had to leave home? Make sure other household members know where everything is.

And set a reminder to revision your records at regular intervals. Steuer, for instance, saves his account statements as PDFs and prints everything out once a year. “One of the massive concerns is that people could conceivably break into your 401(k) and drain your 401(k) account,” he notes. Account statements could help if a hack affects any financial balances.

It all adds up to a web of protection that (hopefully) you’ll never have to use.

“The goal is not to anticipate every scenario,” mentioned Schwab's Dan Stanush, “but to have enough flexibility to meet basic needs while systems come back online.”.

In this episode of Motley Fool Rule Breaker Investing, Motley Fool co-founder David Gardner explores the world of sports betting, discussing the money made, the influence wielded by celebrities, and the legacy left behind.

David Gardner: What if I told you there's an enormously popular way to put your money at risk, where the odds are stacked against you, the middleman takes a cut, and the more you play, the more likely you are to lose? What if some of America's most admired athletes and entertainers were being paid to encourage you to play that game? Well, that's sports betting in America today. This week, I want to talk about the math, the money, and something I care about even more: how we choose to make our money. I'm a believer in freedom, I'm a believer in investing, and I'm a believer that what we do with our influence matters. Sports betting and a few questions for some famous friends only on this week's Rule Breaker Investing.

According to recent reports, welcome back to Rule Breaker Investing. This week, something a little different. I'm going to speak about sports betting. Now, I've spoken about this before. In fact, I devoted a page and a half of my book Rule Breaker Investing to this subject, and I'm going to share that passage with you shortly. But first, why am I returning to it? Well, because sports betting seems to be everywhere these days, and I love sports. I bet you do, too. I've loved sports all my life. Increasingly, when I sit down to watch a football game, a baseball game, or a basketball game these days, I'm reminded that there's another game going on alongside the one that's on the field. Who's favored? What's the spread? What's the over-under? Who's going to score the next touchdown? Of course, would you like to put a little money on that? I find myself wondering whether we've reached a point where the business of betting on sports is beginning to crowd out, for some of us, the simple pleasure of watching sports. Just how significant has this become? Well, according to the American Gaming Association in 2025, Americans placed nearly $167 billion in legal commercial sports bets. Yeah, that's “billion” with a B. How much did the sportsbooks keep after paying out their winners? Nearly $17 billion. That's about $0.10 of every dollar wagered. Think about that. $17 billion flowing net from sports bettors to the companies taking their bets in a single year. That's just sports betting.

Industry observers note that across casinos, online gambling, and sportsbooks, the American commercial gambling industry generated almost $79 billion in revenue last year. There's a latest kid on the block: prediction markets, Kalshi and Polymarket among others. According to Pew Research Center, those two platforms alone recorded $53 billion in worldwide trading volume in July of this year, one month. Now, that's measured differently from sports betting, so we can't simply add those numbers together, yet much of that trading is now focused on sports. My point is simple. This is an enormous business, and it's getting bigger. Those billions flowing to the gambling operators, they're coming from somewhere, from where? From whom? Well, from the customers, their customers, from you. If you're their customer, that's your money they're taking hand over fist. Now, I want to make something clear up front. I believe sports betting should be legal. I've always believed that adults should be free to make our own decisions with our own money. That includes decisions that I might think are foolish. I've enjoyed friendly wagers myself over the years. There's nothing inherently wrong with two friends putting $5 on a game or the loser buying dinner. Yeah, I think there's an enormous difference between that and the industrial-scale business of persuading millions of people to bet and bet again and bet again.

This week, I want to ask three questions. First, what does the math tell us? Second, what distinguishes sports betting from stock market investing? Third, a question that matters very much to me. I hope you, too, does it matter how we make our money? Let's start with a little math. I've often remarked that investing in the stock market is a little like sailing. Imagine you and me sitting together in a sailboat, the wind pushing us forward. Well, that would be the stock market’s compounding positive returns. That wind is at our backs. When you're a stock market investor, the broad stock market consistently rises over time, even with, of course, the storm, and there will always be storms. Sometimes the wind blows right in our faces. Sometimes our boat gets tossed around. Over decades, though, investors have benefited from owning pieces of productive enterprises, companies that create goods and services, generate profits, and grow. Now, sports betting has a fundamentally different mathematical structure. Here's a simple example. Suppose you and I bet on opposite sides of a football game. We each have a 50% chance of winning. If we're just betting against each other, one of us wins, one of us loses. Between us, no wealth has been created.

Now introduce a sportsbook. A common arrangement requires you to risk $110 to win $100. So if you win, you make $100; if you lose, you're out $110. OK, so suppose you make 100 such bets, each one a genuine 50-50 proposition. You win 50 and lose 50. Well, on your 50 winners, you're going to make $5,000, and on your 50 losers, you're going to lose $5,500. Congratulations, you've gotten half your predictions right, and you've lost $500. You're a loser. That's not even including the time and the attention that you devoted to making those bets in the first place, which, by the way, might be just as expensive or even more so. Now, the rare skilled bettor may find favorable odds, and the precise mathematics are going to vary from wager to wager. The point is that the sportsbook’s margin — that middleman is creating a headwind that the typical bettor has to overcome in order just to break even.

In a recent development, and this is where I want to pull a page from my book Rule Breaker Investing. Last September, my book Rule Breaker Investing was published. Part 1 is the six habits of the Rule Breaker Investor. Part 2 is the six traits that we look for in Rule Breaker stocks. Then in Part 3, I discussed the six principles of Rule Breaker portfolio management. One of them, Principle number five, is that you get to invest the whole race, by which I mean that unlike horse race bettors who have to place their bets before the race, we stock market investors can pay attention to our investments over time while we're holding them as part owners and make better decisions as we learn. Here's what I wrote about sports betting, and I quote, "The key to principle number five is simple. Use what's happening in the race to make every additional investment you make during the race smarter.

Industry observers note that this is in contrast to a raging upcoming area of speculation in this era, sports betting, to which I briefly want to speak. Sports betting, of course, is all or nothing, and the bet has to be put down before the game is played. Sports bettors have numerous disadvantages compared to stock market investors. They routinely have to take all-or-nothing propositions. They pay a middleman, the house, up to 10% commission and have to put down all their money before the race or the game starts. It's regrettable how easy and attractive sports betting is made to sound when it's such a losing play, day in and day out. I'm hoping this book reaches many and helps clarify for them why their money is so much better invested in the stock market. The market tends to rise over time, you and me in the sailboat, the wind at our backs. Sports betting, by its nature, is zero-sum, and your expected return is always negative. The handicaps are set very effectively, whether we’re talking about a 6.5-point favorite in basketball or seven-to-five odds at a horse track. One bettor will win, the other will lose, and the house will always take its cut. Over time, almost all consistent sports bettors lose money. What happens to those who consistently invest over time? The difference is immense.

According to recent reports, though sports betting is now widely legal in the U.S., that doesn't make it a smart bet. I've made friendly wagers with friends for decades, which can make watching games more fun and stressful. But I look askance at massive-volume betting and especially its influence on the media coverage of sports I love. A booming gambling industry does not reflect my best vision for our future. Sports betting, as has been mentioned of state lotteries, functions broadly as yet another tax on imbeciles. While some bettors may see it differently, the reality is that over time, most will lose their money." Well, there you have it, my words in print from my book Rule Breaker Investing published a year ago.

Recent findings suggest that two quick clarifications. First, sports betting today does include live betting where you can place wagers while a game is underway. That particular distinction I drew about betting before the game isn't universally true. Second, when I speak about the house taking up to 10%, that's a shorthand for a common betting convention, rather than a universal commission on every dollar wagered. That's strong language. I certainly don't think everyone who places a sports bet is an imbecile. The phrase is intended to make us think about a system in which the average participant faces a mathematical disadvantage and keeps betting over and over. I especially want to add what I consider the biggest distinction between owning stock and making a bet. Even though you often hear people saying, both are just gambling.

The stock market, sports, they are fundamentally different when you own stock, you literally own an asset, part ownership of a domestic or foreign business, you are an owner. You own a piece of an enterprise that may create value for years or, even better, decades. When you make a sports bet, you have a wager on a short-term outcome. You're not an owner of the teams or the underlying economic activity. You're a speculator. You're typically paying a price to an intermediary of the house to make your bet. Over time, the typical bettor, as I stated earlier, is fighting math. Now, I suspect many of those who are fighting math don't fully understand the math that they're fighting. If you add up all the winnings and losses across all the customers and the money that flows to the house, well, it means that collectively, their customers come out behind. Earlier, I mentioned making 100 $100 bets. Let's say you win half of them, so you win $100, 50 times; you lose the other 50. It sounds like breaking even, right? Except you don't. As we pointed out, you've paid the house $500 for the so-called entertainment of breaking even. That's a 5% loss on your $10,000 wager.

Industry observers note that now imagine if you’d simply invested that $10,000 instead: a 50-stock portfolio, $200 in each position, or just simply $10,000 plunked into an index fund. Imagine what happens to that money. It grows over the years, in fits and starts through ups and downs, but with the possibility of compounding into something much bigger. That is the real opportunity cost of sports betting, and it is massive. It's not just the money you lost. It's the wealth you never give yourself the chance to build. The house doesn't win every bet. It doesn't need to.

Industry observers note that its business model is built to win over time. Let me put that larger distinction as simply as I can. In the stock market, your success doesn't require my failure. If you and I both buy shares of a wonderful business and that business grows and prospers for 20 years, we both win, and the employees can win. The customers can win. Society can benefit from what that business creates. That's one of the beautiful things about capitalism at its best. Sports betting, again, a very different enterprise. The bookmaker makes its money by operating a market in wagers, and its customers collectively bear the cost of that business, collectively bear the cost of that business. Latest Update: Should You Buy Nvidia Stock Before CEO Jensen Huang Testifies in Front of Congress on Dec. 1 and Dec. 3?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang may be back as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%), but the chip giant's worries are far from over, as regulators and lawmakers continue to investigate whether Nvidia breached export controls and whether Huang's relationship with a Singaporean data center executive may have posed national security risks.
  • Huang and other Nvidia executives are set to testify before Congress next week on the above concerns, which the entire stock market will be watching.
  • 1, Huang will testify before the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Bram Berkowitz – Nov 27, 2026 at 2:28PM EST.

Jensen Huang may be back as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%), but the chip giant's worries are far from over, as regulators and lawmakers continue to investigate whether Nvidia breached export controls and whether Huang's relationship with a Singaporean data center executive may have posed national security risks.

Huang and other Nvidia executives are set to testify before Congress next week on the above concerns, which the entire stock market will be watching.

It has been revealed that on Dec. 1, Huang will testify before the U.S. House of Representatives' Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committee, and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. Nvidia's General Counsel Tim Teter will also testify before the same committees on Dec. 2. Both hearings will be private, with transcripts not expected to be published publicly for some time.

Recent findings suggest that but on Dec. 3, Huang will testify at a live hearing before the U.S. Senate Banking Committee, an event that will be closely monitored by all investors. Should investors buy Nvidia stock before these hearings?

While President Donald Trump has come out in support of Huang and claims to have played a role in his reinstatement, the hearings will help reveal how other lawmakers feel about Huang and what's going on with Nvidia.

"The market volatility and nervousness is centered on a number of challenges that the Jensen soap opera has highlighted front and center," Yorkville Ives analyst and Managing Partner Dan Ives wrote in a recent research note, according to Business Insider. "Next week Jensen carries the weight of the entire tech sector and AI Revolution thesis when he marches into DC.".

Huang's reinstatement as CEO led to a swift surge in the stock, but since then, shares have been pressured by lingering investor concerns about the company.

Multiple reports suggest that a woman Huang had an affair with, named Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at the Singaporean data center company MegaSpeed, may have facilitated a network that diverted advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese firms.

NASDAQ · As of 1:15 PM ET 11/27/26.

It has been revealed that investors are trying to understand how much prior demand for Nvidia's chips, if any, may have been driven by similar sources. Since the scandal came to light, the U.S. Commerce Department has moved to close loopholes and tighten export controls that may have allowed Chinese firms to access Nvidia chips remotely.

The Commerce Department is now also requiring companies in select countries, such as Singapore and Indonesia, to obtain a license before transferring or reexporting advanced chips from U.S. companies.

In his note, Ives noted he believes the impact on revenue resulting from such export controls is "a containable 15% to 20% at most." Still, that's a significant amount, and while some of it is priced in, Nvidia stock could certainly face more pressure if it believed future demand wouldn't be as strong.

Given that Wall Street analysts like Ives are already contemplating what would happen to Nvidia's revenue if increased export restrictions lower demand, or some sources of demand abroad are closed off, it's clear the market is pricing in at least some of the potential impact.

Still, Wall Street consensus estimates expect Nvidia to earn $16.61 per share on an adjusted basis for its fiscal year 2028 ending in late January 2028. That means Nvidia trades at just 9x forward earnings, so the valuation is attractive.

But as we've seen through this whole debacle, things can change in a hurry, so I would never tell investors to buy a stock based on a near-term event like a Congressional hearing.

In a recent development, with Nvidia trading at a cheap level, I think investors can purchase a position to hold long term. But I do not believe that the majority of a traditional stock portfolio should be concentrated in Nvidia or AI stocks, as much uncertainty remains.

The company is divesting lower-margin regional casinos to refocus capital on its core horse racing and gaming venues. Three key takeaways from the call stand out for long-term investors.

However, management retains statutory authority to shift historical racing machines (HRMs), which are video gaming terminals driven by past race results, and operational licenses across the state to maximize returns in underserved locations.

Sources indicate that ticket sales for the 153rd Kentucky Derby are pacing 25% ahead of last year's rate as customer demand expands. Long-term value relies on pricing power at Churchill Downs Racetrack, expanding historical racing machine floors, and growing the TwinSpires wagering platform.

Management is working to lower bank leverage below 3.0x following casino sales while compounding cash flow across core platforms.

Breaking: Nvidia, Micron, and Sandisk Trade at Half the S&P 500’s Forward P/E. They Are All Genius Buys.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Comparing stocks to an index like the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.60%) is a great way to assess their relative valuation.
  • In a recent development, the same goes with being more expensive.
  • Three that are trading at massive discounts from the S&P 500 are Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%), Sandisk (SNDK +15.96%), and Micron Technology (MU +7.60%).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Keithen Drury – Nov 27, 2026 at 2:38PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

Comparing stocks to an index like the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.60%) is a great way to assess their relative valuation. For example, if a stock is trading at an earnings ratio that’s cheaper than the market average, there should be a good reason for that.

In a recent development, the same goes with being more expensive. What investors should often be looking for is stocks that are not valued marginally above or below the S&P 500, but under it by an amount significant enough to raise eyebrows when the business is assessed.

Three that are trading at massive discounts from the S&P 500 are Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%), Sandisk (SNDK +15.96%), and Micron Technology (MU +7.60%). All three are posting monster growth figures, so if the reasons they trade at a discount don't hold water, then they are well worth buying at these prices.

First, let's look at the forward price-to-earnings ratio of the S&P 500, which is right now 18. With Micron, Sandisk, and Nvidia's fiscal year not ending in the next 12 months exactly, there is a bit of a mismatch on end dates in this analysis. However, the offsetting periods aren’t so large that the difference really matters in this case.

Both Sandisk and Micron are in their fiscal year 2027s right now, and each trades at a substantial discount to the market.

SNDK PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts.

At just 3.6 times forward earnings, Micron looks like a bargain. Sandisk is even cheaper at 2.7 times forward earnings. That means these two are anywhere from five to six times cheaper than the S&P 500 is right now. That's a deep discount, but why do these two trade that low?

Both companies make memory chips, which have two key use cases in AI: providing quick-access memory for computing units and long-term data storage. Demand for these chips from companies building data centers has exceeded the memory industry’s global production capacity. As a result, the memory market is now in a severely supply-constrained state.

Simple economics states that when demand is high and supply is low, prices rise. That is exactly what has happened, and Micron and Sandisk have seen their revenues and profits skyrocket over the past year.

The low prices of these two stocks reflect the market’s bet that these conditions won't last and that a downturn in the memory market is inevitable. However, Micron's management team told investors during its most recent earnings call that it anticipates that memory market conditions will tighten even further in 2027 and 2028. So, these two companies have nothing to worry about in the short term, and that makes their stocks look like absolute bargains in the meantime.

The turmoil around GPU maker Nvidia has been hard to ignore if you're an investor. Furthermore, just because Jensen Huang is back in the CEO role doesn't mean that the manufacturer is in the clear. There are still concerns about whether some of Nvidia’s most powerful processors reached customers in China, despite U.S. trade rules that ban their export to that country.

We'll learn more about what's going on with Nvidia when Huang testifies before Congress, but ongoing investigations could still reveal problems that impact the business.

However, given that Huang was willing to return to the CEO role, I'd say the likelihood of anything too drastic happening is low; otherwise, he might have taken the opportunity to run for the hills.

As a result of its troubles, Nvidia trades at 9.4 times 1-year forward earnings, a low price.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts.

In a recent development, that's about half the price of the S&P 500, but still more expensive than Sandisk or Micron. Regardless, I think all three are worthy buys at this price point, because they are all primed to benefit from the booming AI arms race.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 27, 2026 at 2:46PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Universal Technical Institute ›.

Sources indicate that on its fiscal fourth-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 18, 2026, Universal Technical Institute (UTI +0.95%) announced full-year revenue of $897 million. Expanding campus capacity positions the business to capture rising demand for skilled trades technicians. Three takeaways from the call stand out for long-term investors.

Student demand for technical programs is outpacing available class seats, prompting management to add new schedules and expand facilities. Adding seats to existing campuses helps boost revenue without the full real estate cost of constructing a new location.

Recruiting field bottlenecks in the high school channel hurt student starts during the fourth quarter. Expanding the sales force and restoring centralized training aim to fix those operational stumbles before the next major graduation cycle.

In a recent development, capital expenditures, or cash spent on physical assets, will reach $160 million to $170 million in fiscal 2027 as latest campus introduces accelerate. Pfizer's 6% Yield vs. AbbVie's 53-Year Dividend Streak: Which Stock Is the Better Buy?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:05PM EST.
  • Sources indicate that abbVie's (ABBV -0.88%) 2.3% dividend yield pales in comparison to Pfizer's (PFE +0.21%) 6%.
  • One of the major positives of AbbVie as an investment is that it is a Dividend King.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:05PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than AbbVie ›.

Sources indicate that abbVie's (ABBV -0.88%) 2.3% dividend yield pales in comparison to Pfizer's (PFE +0.21%) 6%. But it is vital to recognize that the average drug organization's yield is only 1.3% and the broader market's yield is just 1%, so AbbVie's yield isn't exactly small. Here's why conservative dividend investors wouldn't be making a mistake by buying AbbVie, but if you can handle a little uncertainty, Pfizer's much higher yield may end up being the better option.

One of the major positives of AbbVie as an investment is that it is a Dividend King. That means that the organization has increased its dividend annually for 50+ consecutive years (53 to be specific), which is not something that happens by accident. It requires a strong business model that is executed well in both good and bad markets. The only problem here is that AbbVie hasn't actually existed for 50 years. It was created in 2013 when it was spun off from Abbott Laboratories (ABT +0.07%). It retained Abbott's dividend record and then, to AbbVie's credit, continued to raise its dividend each year.

Still, it probably isn't appropriate to give AbbVie full credit for its Dividend King status. You should pay extra attention to its actual business, which is well-run and fairly well-positioned. It has strong positions in immunology and oncology. Meanwhile, the drug maker's aesthetics business doesn't face the same patent risks as other drug niches because brand names are vital differentiators. As a business, it is highly desirable.

Recent findings suggest that there's just one small problem: the stock isn't cheap. Its price-to-sales ratio is 7.9x compared to a five-year average of 5.4x. Its price-to-earnings ratio is 50x compared to a five-year average of 41x. You are paying full fair, if not more, for the stock's above-average yield.

NYSE · As of 1:00 PM ET 11/27/26.

Sources indicate that that's where Pfizer starts to look relatively attractive. Not only is its dividend yield likely to be highly attractive to income seekers, but the stock is also much cheaper than AbbVie. Pfizer's 2.5x P/S ratio is in line with its five-year average and far lower than AbbVie's 7.9x. Pfizer's P/E ratio is 40x, which is biased higher by one-time charges and still lower than AbbVie's 50x. If you use the $3.00 per share midpoint of Pfizer's 2026 adjusted earnings guidance, the P/E is around 10x. That's below the stock's nearly 14x five-year average.

A substantial yield from a cheap stock will likely have more appeal than a smaller yield from an expensive stock for most investors. But there are issues to consider, most notably Pfizer's upcoming patent expirations in 2028 (Eliquis) and 2031 (Vyndamax). Those are big deals and will likely result in a substantial decline in revenues and earnings. The thing is, patent expirations are entirely normal in the pharmaceutical sector. Pfizer is working hard to develop fresh drugs to offset the hit, but sometimes the timing doesn't perfectly align.

NYSE · As of 1:01 PM ET 11/27/26.

Industry observers note that still, given the firm's strong history, which dates back to the mid-1800s, it seems highly likely that it will manage this patent expiration cycle, just as it has many times before. As for the dividend, the company is publicly supportive of it and continues to tell investors that its long-term goal is to grow the payment. And even if there were a 50% dividend cut, which seems like a reasonable worst-case scenario, the yield would still be higher than AbbVie's 2.3%.

If you are a risk-averse investor who simply can't tolerate any kind of uncertainty, AbbVie is a perfectly fine, though perhaps expensive, stock to buy. However, Pfizer's higher yield and more attractive valuation will probably make it a better option, assuming you believe it can muddle through its patent-expiration challenges, as it has many times before. Indeed, the risk-versus-reward balance is likely tilted toward reward for long-term dividend investors.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 on Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the firm "has its own China problem.".

    Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.

    Recent findings suggest that the report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the firm kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers.".

    CNBC did not independently verify this information.

    Hunterbrook also mentioned that newly introduced export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips.".

    Recent findings suggest that the allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.

    "The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson stated in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.".

    Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.

    AMD continued to slide after hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (611 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Rheinmetall reins in growth ambitions as Europe's rearmament boom hits hurdles

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Rheinmetall is adopting a more "cautious" approach after the German arms maker lost a major contract to build F126 warships for the country's military, in what would have been Rheinmetall's biggest order since World War II.
    • The tank and ammunition maker now expects sales of between 33 and 37 billion euros (between $36.2 billion and $40.6 billion) by 2030, down from a previous forecast of about 45 billion euros, it told investors at its Capital Markets Day on Friday.
    • That guidance incorporates a "more prudent approach" for its large vehicle systems and weapons and ammunition businesses.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rheinmetall is adopting a more "cautious" approach after the German arms maker lost a major contract to build F126 warships for the country's military, in what would have been Rheinmetall's biggest order since World War II.

    The tank and ammunition maker now expects sales of between 33 and 37 billion euros (between $36.2 billion and $40.6 billion) by 2030, down from a previous forecast of about 45 billion euros, it told investors at its Capital Markets Day on Friday.

    That guidance incorporates a "more prudent approach" for its large vehicle systems and weapons and ammunition businesses.

    CEO Armin Papperger said a 2-billion-euro reduction in the 2030 sales target for its vehicle systems business was a strategic decision to build in a "buffer" against potential project delays and supply chain disruptions, rather than a reflection of further lost contracts or weakening demand.

    It follows a full-year 2026 guidance cut earlier this month, which sent shares down 16% as the organization cited delays to military contracts and ammunition deliveries.

    "The opportunity has not changed; the way we proposal for it has," Rheinmetall mentioned in a organization presentation.

    "We are becoming more cautious whilst retaining our agility in a dynamic market," it said, highlighting a "fresh normal level of conservatism and recalibrated ambition" in the mid-term.

    Shares rose 4% in mid-morning trading amid a European defense sector firmly in the green.

    It has been revealed that rheinmetall and the wider defense industry have benefitted massively from European governments' efforts to rearm amid the war in Ukraine and uncertain security guarantees from the U.S. As governments ramp up military spending to meet NATO's hiked spending targets, defense companies see swelling order books but also struggle to meet soaring demand.

    While shares of Rheinmetall have averaged triple-digit gains between 2022 and 2025, they are down 49% year-to-date. Addressing capital markets specifically, Papperger said he understood the disappointment, but that the loss of the major F126 was "a political thing.".

    "The government made this decision, and the minister made that decision," he mentioned.

    Other headwinds for Rheinmetall in 2026 were an explosion at an ammunition factory in Murcia, Spain, in January, and delays to Germany's Arminius project, a major military procurement program for Boxer armored vehicles, which is now expected to be commissioned next year.

    Papperger remarked delays were due to price negotiations with the government. "I could have the contract immediately if I would reduce the prices, he said.

    "We are fighting hard to get this contract, and we are fighting hard, not only to get the contract, but to make it also profitable.".

    RBC Capital analysts called the lowered mid-term targets a "widely expected reset" with "a general dose of conservatism.".

    "[The] emphasis on digitalisation offerings and the broadness of the portfolio should also help address sentiment around Rheinmetall being an "old-tech" name in a "new-tech" paradigm," the analysts added.

    Some investors are now questioning what role legacy defense contractors like Rheinmetall, BAE Systems, and Leonardo will play in an evolving military context, increasingly focused on technology, autonomous systems, and drones.

    Papperger pushed back on the idea that drones will render traditional military equipment obsolete, arguing that militaries must still replace their aging fleets and maintain the ability to transport troops on the battlefield.

    It has been revealed that "Don't believe what a lot of people [are] telling you in the narrative 'we only need drones.' Forget about that," Papperger noted. "The market potential is still there.".

    Rheinmetall on Friday also warned that Europe faces mounting security threats beyond conventional warfare, pointing to an increase in hybrid attacks ranging from industrial sabotage and cyber espionage to airspace disruption and satellite jamming.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Lee Samaha – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:27PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›.

    Shares in Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +4.83%) rose by 5% at 1 p.m. today as the market continued to digest a couple of positive news developments for the manufacturer. The first is CEO Elon Musk's pledge to give every child in the U.S. two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from Musk personally. The second is the news that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) granted SpaceX the authority to deploy 1 million data centers in space.

    The proposal to gift shares is not only a huge display of generosity by Musk, but also creates significant goodwill around the organization and strengthens public awareness of what SpaceX is doing in the space and AI industries.

    NASDAQ · As of 1:00 PM ET 11/27/26.

    Those aims are also strengthened by the FCC announcement, which clears a path for orbital data centers that SpaceX's management believes it could deploy as early as 2028. The idea is that the cost of orbital data centers will inevitably fall as rocket technology becomes more productive. Furthermore, orbital data centers don't face the power bottlenecks that many data centers do right now.

    Orbital data centers address rising real estate, construction, and power costs and avoid the permitting challenges that terrestrial data centers are increasingly facing. In addition, since Musk believes the price of compute will rise, revenue from orbital data centers may increase while costs decrease.

    It's a key part of SpaceX's long-term growth program, and the FCC decision is a positive result. Still, there are many question marks around their ultimate deployment, not least the key question of how many years orbital data centers will actually be productive, given the likelihood that they won't be serviceable. Something to think about.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:44PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Advanced Micro Devices ›.

    Recent findings suggest that following the takedown of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, a short-seller has decided to go after rival Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +4.56%)based on allegations that the company's chips are also being illegally directed to China. The report sent AMD shares plunging 20% in the two days following the short attack.

    NASDAQ · As of 1:15 PM ET 11/27/26.

    In its report, Hunterbrook Media, which is short AMD stock, claimed that the company is supplying support to its graphics processing units (GPUs) to banned Chinese companies. It alleged that U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems was continuing to get firmware updates that allowed it to use its chips on its servers. It also stated that it gets around 20% of its revenue from customers in China and Hong Kong and that a Chinese partner finishes these chips.

    Industry observers note that however, the short-seller admitted that its own research didn't find any actual export-law violations. It added that it does not know how IEIT got AMD's code or whether it has a license for the firmware. So basically, it's accusing AMD of something with no proof, while saying it's actually not accusing it.

    Overall, the short report is pretty flimsy; however, the market has been so on edge following the Nvidia news, and with artificial intelligence (AI) stocks in general struggling, Hunterbrook took advantage of the situation to try to make a quick buck.

    For its part, AMD said that it "complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across [its] global operations." Otherwise, it did not engage with the short-seller regarding its accusations.

    The chipmaker is allowed to sell its server central processing units (CPUs) in China, as well as certain older-generation GPUs to some Chinese customers, for which it has an export license.

    The sell-off in AMD is a compelling entry point, in my view. The firm is riding two huge waves with inference and agentic AI that should drive significant growth over the next few years.

    In a recent development, AMD has built its latest Helios system, which combines its GPUs and CPUs, around inference and agentic AI. Its chiplet GPU design, which can be packaged with more memory, is ideal for inference.

    Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the company has made some interesting acquisitions that could eventually push this further in future rack-scale solutions. This includes its purchase of predictive memory optimization company MEXT, and Taalas, which makes chips where specific AI models are embedded into them to speed up inference.

    Sources indicate that the launch of Helios comes at an opportune time, with Anthropic recently demonstrating that its Mythos Claude model could switch running models on Nvidia GPUs to AMD GPUs in just a few days. This could significantly weaken Nvidia's CUDA software moat at a time when AMD is just starting to ship Helios to large customers, including OpenAI, Meta Platforms, and Anthropic. With Helios costing nearly half of Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform per gigawatt, AMD has the potential to take significant share in the inference market over the next few years.

    On top of that, the tech giant is just starting to ride a huge wave with agentic AI for its server CPUs. AI agents require a significant amount of high-performance CPUs, which is a market AMD has been taking share in for years. The company's CPUs are helping run Meta's Muse AI agents, and it even has a foothold in Alphabet's lucrative tensor processing unit (TPU) architecture due to its strong security features, with its chips being chosen over Alphabet's own ARM-based CPUs.

    Overall, AMD has a huge growth opportunity, and I'd use this pullback to buy the dip.

    • SAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as the German firm reshapes its software business for the artificial intelligence era, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter.
    • "The business environment in which we operate is changing rapidly through AI, and we are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful," SAP said in a statement to CNBC.
    • Recent findings suggest that "As part of this ongoing transformation, roles and functions will naturally change over time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    SAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as the German firm reshapes its software business for the artificial intelligence era, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter.

    "The business environment in which we operate is changing rapidly through AI, and we are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful," SAP said in a statement to CNBC.

    Recent findings suggest that "As part of this ongoing transformation, roles and functions will naturally change over time. Beyond this, no decisions have been made regarding any further measures. We do not comment on speculation.".

    The company did not provide any further details on potential job cuts.

    The report came as the organization flagged a cybersecurity attack, but stated it had found "no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data.".

    "SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services," a manufacturer spokesperson mentioned.

    Recent findings suggest that "Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on.".

    In a recent development, other software companies have also tied workforce reductions to AI initiatives, though for different reasons. WiseTech Global said in February it planned to cut about 2,000 jobs over two years as it integrated AI into its products and operations.

    Atlassian noted in March it would cut about 1,600 jobs partly to fund further AI investment, while Cloudflare said in May it would eliminate more than 1,100 roles as it moved toward an AI-first operating model.

    Recent findings suggest that in the U.S., employers cited AI in 121,401 job-cut announcements through October 2026, accounting for about 20% of the total, according to a Nov. 5 report from outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

    Industry observers note that SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide. Bloomberg reported that all departments had been asked to identify potential cuts, with product, engineering and sales in particular focus.

    The company also underwent a reorganization in 2024, when it eliminated around 10,000 positions through a program that relied mainly on voluntary departures and retraining.

    Its headcount later remained relatively flat as it hired for latest roles, Bloomberg reported.

    In 2023, SAP CEO Christian Klein told CNBC he did not necessarily expect a reduction in the workforce, saying he expected the firm to grow and "accelerate" its total revenue.

    It has been revealed that the reported cuts come as Klein pushes SAP toward an AI-first strategy. This year, SAP completed four acquisitions — Reltio, Dremio, Prior Labs and TechWolf — and made strategic investments in AI-focused companies including Parloa, n8n and Conduct.

    The acquisitions are intended to help SAP organize company data, develop AI models for business information and analyze workforce skills.

    Anthropic Stock Is Up 11% From Its IPO Price, and One Analyst Still Sees 63% Upside. Should You Buy?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Anthropic (ANT +10.98%) went public on Nov.
    • Wall Street's analysts have been weighing in, and so far they're pretty bullish.
    • In a recent development, one detail makes those calls more interesting than usual: none of the three firms is named anywhere in Anthropic's prospectus, which lists 22 banks on its cover.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 27, 2026 at 4:03PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

    Anthropic (ANT +10.98%) went public on Nov. 19 at $83 a share, raising $81.3 billion in one of the largest initial public offerings ever. After a wild first week, in which the stock opened at $111.50 and later closed below its offering price, it finished Friday at $91.88, about 11% above its IPO price.

    Wall Street's analysts have been weighing in, and so far they're pretty bullish. Wedbush rated the stock outperform with a $120 price target. Canaccord rated it a buy with a $135 target. Oppenheimer is among the highest, with an outperform rating and a $150 target, roughly 63% above current levels.

    In a recent development, one detail makes those calls more interesting than usual: none of the three firms is named anywhere in Anthropic's prospectus, which lists 22 banks on its cover. Analysts at a deal's underwriters tend to start coverage with positive ratings, but these three had no apparent direct role in the offering.

    Dario Amodei. Image source: Getty Images.

    Sources indicate that the bull case starts with growth that's hard to find anywhere else among AI stocks. According to its prospectus, Anthropic's revenue rose from $1.4 billion in the third quarter of 2025 to $17 billion in the third quarter of 2026. Multiply that latest quarter by four, and the company is running at nearly $68 billion a year in sales.

    It has been revealed that the analysts' argument is that this is still early. Canaccord noted it is "increasingly convinced that the opportunity is considerably larger than traditional software spending." Software that completes tasks on its own can be paid for from the money companies spend on people, a far larger pool than the money they spend on software. Wedbush pointed to the "global knowledge wage pool" as the prize. Oppenheimer's target is built on a forecast of $275.1 billion in revenue in 2028, with operating margins above 20%.

    Sources indicate that the business is also less dependent on a handful of substantial buyers than you might expect. No customer accounted for more than 10% of revenue in the first nine months of 2026, and about 79% of third-quarter revenue came from customers outside the top five.

    Three things in the filing deserve a hard look before you buy.

    First, profits are uneven. Anthropic earned an operating profit of $974 million in the second quarter of 2026, then slipped back to a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter as computing costs jumped 77% to $9.9 billion. (Its far larger reported net losses mostly reflect accounting charges on convertible securities.).

    In a recent development, second, the spending commitments are enormous. Anthropic indicates it has signed up for about $900.9 billion of spending commitments, substantially all of it for computing and infrastructure, with $451.6 billion expected before the end of 2030 and $70.7 billion due within 12 months of Sept. 30. That next-year bill is roughly equal to its current annual revenue pace. Many of these contracts require payment whether or not the capacity gets used, so if demand cools, the costs won't shrink with it.

    Third, the valuation already assumes a lot. With about 13.2 billion shares outstanding after the IPO, Anthropic is worth roughly $1.2 trillion, or about 18 times its annualized revenue. To grow into Oppenheimer's 2028 forecast, revenue would need to roughly quadruple from today's pace in about two years.

    If you believe AI will take on a growing share of white-collar work, Anthropic is one of the most direct ways to own that trend, and its growth so far supports the analysts' optimism. But at roughly 18 times sales, with hundreds of billions in fixed commitments ahead, the stock leaves little room for a stumble.

    A sensible approach is to start small and build the position over time, for example by buying a set dollar amount each month while the insider unlocks play out through next spring. That way, a sell-off when insiders become free to sell becomes a chance to buy more rather than a reason to panic. Investors who want AI exposure with less risk tied to one company may prefer to keep Anthropic as a modest slice of a broader portfolio of tech stocks.

    Prescription volumes continue to build across expanding physician networks, and management isn't hiding its satisfaction with the momentum.

    Dosing flexibility and 94% gross margins drive durable operational leverage. Management is strategically tracking referral recovery, conversion stability, and trial enrollment across upcoming indications.

    Liquidia ended the quarter with $396.1 million in cash before its settlement obligations, most of which are payable in cash through April 2027.

    Industry News: Carnival Just Filed Something Revealing the Day After Thanksgiving. Should You Buy the Stock?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that companies don't usually announce good news in a compensation filing on the Friday after Thanksgiving.
    • In August 2022, Carnival's board gave CEO Josh Weinstein a special grant of 500,000 restricted stock units.
    • Sources indicate that when the board set those goals, Carnival was still working its way back from the pandemic shutdown that had idled its fleet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 27, 2026 at 4:26PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Carnival Corp. ›.

    Industry observers note that companies don't usually announce good news in a compensation filing on the Friday after Thanksgiving. But a regulatory filing that Carnival (CCL +0.54%) released on Friday contains one of the clearest signals yet about the cruise operator's recovery.

    In August 2022, Carnival's board gave CEO Josh Weinstein a special grant of 500,000 restricted stock units. The award could pay out anywhere from zero to twice that amount in February 2028, depending on Carnival's average adjusted return on invested capital (ROIC) in fiscal 2026 and 2027. ROIC measures how much profit a organization squeezes out of the money tied up in its business, which for a cruise line means a lot of very expensive ships.

    Sources indicate that when the board set those goals, Carnival was still working its way back from the pandemic shutdown that had idled its fleet. According to the filing, the award was nonetheless projected to pay out at the maximum level of 200% under its original terms.

    Industry observers note that on Nov. 24, the compensation committee changed the deal. The performance period now ends this Nov. 30 instead of a year later, and the award will vest on Dec. 21. At the same time, the committee raised the bar: the ROIC goal is now tougher than originally set, two other targets tied to 2026 earnings and emissions were added, and the maximum payout was cut to 180%, or 900,000 shares. That's worth about $25 million at Friday's price of $28.26. The filing doesn't explain why the cap was lowered, but the effect is that Weinstein gives up as many as 100,000 shares in exchange for being paid more than a year earlier. He also has to hold the shares he receives after taxes until December 2028 and must return them if he quits before the original 2028 vesting date.

    The details of executive pay can be a red flag. Here, the more telling point is the one buried in the middle: four years ago, the board set return targets for 2026 and 2027, and Carnival has been on track to beat them by enough to max out the award.

    In a recent development, carnival's latest results back that up. In its fiscal third quarter, which ended Aug. 31, the manufacturer reported record revenue of $8.4 billion and record net income of $1.9 billion. Customer deposits, a sign of future demand, hit a third-quarter record of $7.6 billion. Management said bookings for 2027 are at record levels for both occupancy and pricing.

    Industry observers note that the organization is also spending its cash on shareholders and on its balance sheet. Carnival had repurchased about $1.2 billion of stock through late September this year and paid out $618 million in dividends in the first nine months of the fiscal year, after paying none in the same period a year earlier. Total debt fell to $24.6 billion as of Aug. 31, down from $27.4 billion at the end of the prior fiscal year, and S&P upgraded the company to investment-grade during the quarter.

    It has been revealed that for the full fiscal year ending this month, Carnival expects adjusted earnings of about $2.24 per share. At $28.15, the stock trades at roughly 13 times that figure, below its 52-week high of $34.03.

    There are real risks. Higher fuel prices and currency moves cut about $0.10 per share from third-quarter adjusted earnings, and the company cited additional costs due to disruptions related to the Middle East conflict. Debt is falling but still large, and cruising is the kind of discretionary spending families cut first in a downturn.

    Still, the compensation filing adds something you don't often get: evidence that Carnival's own targets, set when the outlook was far murkier, turned out to be easy. For investors looking at travel stocks, a company delivering record profits, shrinking its debt, and paying a dividend again at about 13 times earnings looks like a reasonable buy.     #166661. Tech Report: Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (750 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S.
    • The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.
    • Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a substantial win for the firm and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.

    The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.

    It wasn't supposed to play out this way.

    Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.

    Industry observers note that some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

    In a recent development, adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.

    Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech.

    But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.

    Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year.

    Sources indicate that "You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.

    Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes.

    Recent findings suggest that "The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3.".

    While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.

    Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market.

    "There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets.

    Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.

    Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.

    A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the tech giant in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade.

    "If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday.".

    For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks.

    Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.

    Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com, viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.

    In a recent development, one bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.

    — CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

    Planes, trains and automobiles: The best ways to beat travel fatigue—so you can come home feeling rested and fulfilled

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that five-hour flights.
    • It has been revealed that an estimated 81.5 million Americans are projected to travel, or have already traveled, at least 50 miles from their homes between Nov.
    • High gas prices and soaring plane ticket costs may factor into the shift.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that five-hour flights. Eleven-hour road trips. Fifteen-hour train rides. All potentially exhausting options for the annual tradition of convening around the dinner table with loved ones on Thanksgiving.

    It has been revealed that an estimated 81.5 million Americans are projected to travel, or have already traveled, at least 50 miles from their homes between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30, according to the American Automobile Association. And their mode of transportation is shifting: Fewer people are flying or driving this year compared to 2025, and more are traveling by buses, trains and cruises, AAA data shows.

    High gas prices and soaring plane ticket costs may factor into the shift. As of Wednesday evening, fuel prices are roughly 17% higher than they were on the same date in 2025, according to AAA data. Meanwhile, "months of elevated jet fuel costs due to the conflict in Iran have contributed to Thanksgiving and Christmas airfares reaching 10-year highs," according to fare-tracking platform Hopper.

    The alternate modes of transit may open travelers up to fresh experiences — and new forms of travel fatigue to keep you from returning home feeling rested and fulfilled. You're probably already familiar with the exhaustion you might get from a day of plane travel, for example. In airplanes, "there can be lower humidity, maybe lower oxygen levels at cabin pressure. Sometimes people report feeling more dehydrated or drained. You're adjusting to that change in altitude," says Alaina Tiani, a Cleveland Clinic behavioral sleep medicine psychologist.

    But even waiting in places like train stations or cruise ports can feel draining due to sheer sensory overload, Tiani claims. And then, depending on your mode of travel, you may still need to deal with cramped seating and limited ability to get up and walk around or drink some water and eat a snack.

    Once you arrive at your destination, managing responsibilities like remembering where you put your hotel key and deciding what to eat and how to structure your day can also take a mental toll, states travel writer Shannon O'Donnell, who's written about managing travel fatigue. "All of that actually requires a lot more thinking and planning for your brain," she says, adding: "People just don't understand how those add up and why a relaxing vacation suddenly has them feeling wrecked.".

    According to recent reports, the consequences can sneak up on you, O'Donnell notes. Travel fatigue can "present as maybe a lack of interest in something that you might usually find fascinating," she states. Instead of looking out the window on a plane ride or playing car games with your kids on a road trip, you might disengage and appear apathetic to the people around you.

    Industry observers note that you might stand a better chance of a fulfilling, restful holiday if you prepare for your travel fatigue. Here, Tiani and O'Donnell share their advice for how to do it:.

    Is Anthropic Stock a Buy Before Its Dec. 15 Share Unlock?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Anthropic (ANT +10.98%) closed below its $83 initial public offering (IPO) price for the first time on Tuesday, Nov.
    • FTSE Russell has noted Anthropic will join the Russell 1000 after the close on Friday, Dec.
    • 15 isn't the first chance for insiders to sell.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Daniel Sparks – Nov 27, 2026 at 4:37PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

    Anthropic (ANT +10.98%) closed below its $83 initial public offering (IPO) price for the first time on Tuesday, Nov. 24. On Wednesday, Nov. 25, it traded as low as $73.85 and closed at $82.79.

    FTSE Russell has noted Anthropic will join the Russell 1000 after the close on Friday, Dec. 11, and the Nasdaq-100 might follow at the open on Monday, Dec. 21. In between, on Tuesday, Dec. 15, up to 303 million shares become sellable in the next scheduled release under Anthropic's lockup agreements (deals that ban existing holders from selling for fixed periods).

    Could the index buying offset that new supply?

    Dec. 15 isn't the first chance for insiders to sell. Under Anthropic's lockup terms, employees, consultants, and some officers and directors could sell up to 315 million shares starting the first day of trading.

    In a recent development, the Dec. 15 release covers a group of existing investors, with up to 303 million shares becoming sellable then, another 303 million on Jan. 5, 353 million on Jan. 19, and 353 million more on Feb. 2. All told, up to around 1.3 billion shares might become sellable over seven weeks -- more than the 1.1 billion or so sold in the IPO. At Wednesday's close, the Dec. 15 release alone would be worth around $25 billion.

    Industry observers note that then the releases grow. Up to 1.7 billion shares become sellable just after Anthropic posts full-year 2026 results, on a date it hasn't set, and up to 2.4 billion more follow in the next 10 weeks or so. The largest single release, up to 3.0 billion shares, comes after the first-quarter 2027 report or by mid-May 2027 at the latest.

    Recent findings suggest that sure, not all eligible shares will be sold. But each date offers early holders a fresh chance to sell, with the growth stock already under what IPO buyers paid.

    Sources indicate that anthropic's Nasdaq-100 entry is still a projection. Under Nasdaq's rules, an IPO whose full market value ranks among the index's 40 largest members normally joins after 15 trading days. But Anthropic's seventh trading day, Monday, Nov. 30, is also the ranking date for the index's yearly reshuffle, which Nasdaq is set to announce after the close on Dec. 11. That would put Anthropic in the reshuffle, effective at the open on Dec. 21.

    It has been revealed that even then, the index wouldn't weight Anthropic at its $1.1 trillion valuation. Nasdaq leaves unlisted shares, like Anthropic's nonvoting Class N stock, out of its weighting. And for a firm with under a third of its shares trading freely, it counts up to three times the free-floating shares. If it counts just the shares sold in the IPO, Anthropic would be weighted as if it were worth around $280 billion.

    According to recent reports, nasdaq's own example of a hypothetical $1 trillion IPO with 6% of its shares floated came to about $6 billion of buying, assuming funds tracking the index had $600 billion. Anthropic's capped value is over 50% bigger than the example's $180 billion, so on the same assumptions I'd put its fund buying around $9 billion, well below the value of the Dec. 15 release.

    It has been revealed that index funds must hold a stock when its addition takes effect. So Russell 1000 funds would probably buy at the close on Dec. 11, and Nasdaq-100 funds like the Invesco QQQ Trust at the close before Dec. 21. Then, their buying would mostly track fund inflows and any gain in Anthropic's index weight at a quarterly review.

    NASDAQ · As of 1:15 PM ET 11/27/26.

    The next massive releases, up to about 4.1 billion shares in all, are linked to Anthropic's full-year 2026 results, which will include a holiday quarter. In its prospectus, the AI organization said usage tends to drop around holidays, and total customer spend fell about 20% in the two weeks ending Jan. 2, 2026, compared to the two weeks before.

    Its last holiday quarter also had the slowest sequential growth in 2025. Revenue for the fourth quarter climbed 48% over the previous quarter, after a 76% gain a quarter earlier. Growth was already down to 47% by the third quarter of 2026, and the company expects seasonal effects to get more noticeable as its growth rate falls.

    In the end, I don't think the index buying can soak up much of that supply. The funds buy once and may finish by Dec. 21, but the releases run through February and grow after the full-year 2026 report. For a buyer around the $83 IPO price, I'd rather watch how the stock holds up through the January releases first. And, of course, I'd also keep an eye on the underlying business, looking to see if it can live up to its wild valuation.

    In a recent development, imagine a property manager staring at a mountain of unpaid invoices and frustrated residents, manually typing every detail into a legacy spreadsheet that crashes once a week. Now, picture that same manager clicking a single button in AppFolio (APPF +1.48%) to automate the entire workflow. As of Nov. 19, 2026, the stock trades at $207.83, reflecting a turbulent period where it has fallen 7% over the past year despite consistent, double-digit growth in its core operational metrics.

    According to recent reports, our proprietary Hidden Gems scoring system assigns AppFolio an overall Superscore of 86 out of 100, placing it in the Strong category. The Superscore is an AI-powered score that evaluates a company's overall strength by combining financial performance, product market position, technological capabilities, leadership quality, and relative valuation. It represents the unification of all our scores into a single score for public companies, with five rating bands: Exceptional (90-100), Strong (75-89), Above Average (60-74), Average (40-59), and Cautious (0-39). This analysis pairs the reasons the score is high with the reasons it is not higher so you can weigh both sides of the business before doing more work.

    NASDAQ · As of 1:00 PM ET 11/27/26.

    AppFolio is a highly capital-efficient business, earning outsize profits on a small base of tangible assets. This efficiency helps it turn each point of revenue growth into stronger returns, which is why the market is willing to pay a premium for the stock. This efficiency does not eliminate valuation risk, but it does suggest that the company's growth is inherently more valuable than that of a less efficient, capital-heavy competitor.

    This stock warrants a closer look if...

    AppFolio operates a cloud-based platform for property managers across single-family, multifamily, affordable, commercial, student housing, and community associations. Its asset-light vertical SaaS Platform and wide range of property categories means it doesn't need to bet on a specific segment of the real estate market in order to succeed. It generates steady recurring revenue from subscriptions and benefits from high switching costs -- once a property manager moves accounting, leases, and resident workflows onto the platform, switching service providers is pretty unappealing.

    Its third-quarter results were strong and its balance sheet remains solid. AppFolio reported 19% year-over-year revenue growth and 8% growth in portfolios under management in Q3. Operating cash flow was approximately $96.8 million, up 12.51% year over year. Operating income grew more than twice as fast as revenue, and the manufacturer has no debt on its balance sheet.

    Sources indicate that and the growth runway could be long. A recent study released by the company in partnership with the Institute of Real Estate Management (IREM) revealed that adoption of AI in real estate is "steady rather than explosive," and that real estate management still lags other industries in terms of overall adoption. AppFolio was the first to offer embedded generative AI for property management and is recognized as one of the most heavily AI-embedded major residential property management platforms, giving it an early-mover advantage as generative AI adoption increases both in general and within the real estate industry.

    Despite its premium valuation, the stock has a consensus buy rating and an average price target of $250, indicating possible upside of 16%.

    It has been revealed that finally, industry uncertainty has likely contributed to Sandisk's P/E ratio falling to just 5.5. Even with doubts about AI growth, that low valuation probably meant a stock price recovery was inevitable.
